newsitem.title: ALBANIA: U.S. marines rescue Americans from Albania anarchy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. marines rescue Americans from Albania anarchy.

text.p: Huge Sea Stallion helicopters hugged the countryside, machinegunners scanning the rocky terrain, as U.S. marines swept in on Saturday to rescue Americans from Albania's civil chaos.
Units of heavily-armed marines guarded the landing site on the outskirts of Tirana while armour-packed Cobra combat helicopters buzzed surrounding buildings to ward off attack from gun-toting locals.
The Cobras' forward cannons pointed menacingly towards the houses.
The moment the grey Sea Stallions touched down, a stream of foreigners, including young children and an old man carried on a stretcher, were rushed aboard.

Within minutes, the helicopters lifted off from the diplomatic compound, raising huge clouds of dust as they swung out on the return journey across the Adriatic sea to air bases in Italy's southeast heel.
A total of 739 people from 32 countries were airlifted out of Albania during the first three days of the U.S. evacuation, codenamed Silver Wake.

"The operation will carry on until our ambassador here tells us to stop," said Colonel Emerson Gardner, who heads the marine mission organised from the amphibious assault ship USS Nassau off the Albanian coast.
The operation, suspended on Friday after two Cobras came under fire, restarted at dawn on Saturday.

Gunshots crackled around the grassy U.S. diplomatic housing compound, where the helicopters arrived, as unseen rebels in surrounding hills fired round after round from their recently-looted automatic weapons.
"They're going to melt the barrels of their guns soon," said a 33-year-old marine from Florida.
Marine officers said the helicopters were fired at on Friday as they flew over Tirana to pick up another batch of evacuees. One Cobra swiftly replied with its 20mm guns to "pacify" the situation.
"We are not able to sanitise this area, in other words remove all weaponry, but we think we've got any risk supressed. We've got it under control," Gardner told reporters.
Soldiers patrolled the exposed compound in jeeps weighed down by heavy 50mm machine guns. Marksmen lay hidden besides the bright white buildings or tucked in behind sandbags.

Foreigners were swiftly checked out by consular officials. Anyone without proper papers was turned away at the gates where a handful of Albanian plainclothes police brandishing guns were on hand to prevent trouble.

"The situation is wild out there," said Eddie Drishti, a young American student who had been visting relatives in Albania. "There's no stability, no government, just shooting and looting. I had to get out."
The helicopter shuttle stopped after dark as the shooting intensified and streams of small orange tracers filled the sky.
"The sky gets lit up like Christmas trees. Sometimes they fire off whole magazines of tracers," said Lance Corporal Desmond Bryant, from the U.S. state of Georgia.
Soldiers said the rebels invariably fired into the air, with some of the spent bullets falling back to earth inside the fenced-off compound, but they said they did not feel threatened.
"We expected World War Three and instead got a picnic in a park," said one nonchalant soldier from Carolina.
